prompt: Why is self-consistency pointless with greedy decoding?
options: Greedy decoding returns the same chain every time, so there is nothing to vote over
Greedy decoding never produces a final answer
explanation: Voting needs diverse samples; temperature and top-p sampling provide them.

prompt: Five samples give the final answers 7, 7, 3, 7, 9. What does plurality voting return?
options: No answer because 7 is not a majority of the answer space
explanation: 7 has three votes against one each; plurality only needs the largest count.

prompt: Each sample is correct with probability $p=0.6$ and every wrong sample gives the same wrong answer. What is the probability that a vote of $n=3$ samples is correct? (decimal)
Under the single-wrong-answer binomial model, what happens to voting accuracy as $n\to\infty$ when $p=0.4$?
explanation: The fraction of correct samples concentrates at 0.4 < 1/2, so the wrong answer almost surely has more than half of the votes.

prompt: Why can plurality voting help on a problem with $p=0.3$ even though a majority vote would not?
options: Because the wrong samples may be split over many different answers, so the correct one only needs the largest count
Because plurality voting ignores wrong answers
explanation: With scattered wrong answers (for example four equally likely ones) the correct answer at 30% is the mode and wins often (about 0.43 at n = 9).

prompt: Book table: 33.4% accuracy at 129.2 min (one sample) and 42.2% at 211.6 min ($n=3$). What is the marginal gain in accuracy points per extra minute? (three decimals)
Which statement about best-of-n with a scorer is correct?
options: It equals pass@n only if the scorer is a perfect verifier; at answer time the scorer is usually just a proxy and can be fooled
It is always worse than voting
It needs a reference answer at inference time
explanation: A perfect verifier would keep any correct sample (pass@n). Real scorers (heuristics, confidence, judges) are imperfect.

prompt: With top-p = 0.8 and sorted probabilities 0.45, 0.28, 0.08, 0.07, ..., which tokens does the book's rule (keep while the mass BEFORE the token is below top-p) keep?
explanation: Mass before token 3 is 0.73 < 0.8, so it is kept; before token 4 it is 0.81 >= 0.8, so tokens 4 and later are dropped.

prompt: The book's results for top-p + self-consistency without CoT are 29.6%, 27.8%, 31.6% for n = 3, 5, 10. What is the most sensible reading?
options: Voting got worse from 3 to 5 samples
Differences of 2 to 3 points on 500 problems are comparable to the standard error, so no ordering can be concluded
Accuracy must be monotone in n, so the data are wrong
explanation: The standard error is about 2 points; moreover correlated mistakes limit the benefit. Do not read a trend into noise.
